items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I move, That the Land
Transport Management Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  It is my intention to
nominate the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee to consider the bill.
This bill will amend the Land Transport Management Act 2003. The Act provides
the planning and funding framework that channels around $3 billion of central
government funding each year into road construction and maintenance, and public
transport. The bill is part of the Govern ment’s ongoing efforts to cut unnecessary red
tape and create a better, more effective legislative framework for transport. The bill will
lead to streamlined decision-making and fewer prescriptive planning processes for those
in the transport sector. It will allow councils greater flexibility to plan for the needs of
their region, and it will en sure that both central governme nt and local government get
better value for money from their investments in public transport.
5102 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 11 Sep 2012
The bill has three main components. First,  it will remedy some problems with the
planning and funding framework for the La nd Transport Management Act 2003. That
framework imposes processes th at are duplicative, repetiti ve, and prescriptive, which
leads to uncertainty, excessive paperwork, and unnecessary compliance costs. The bill
will make the Act easier to use and understand by focusing its purpose and decision-
making criteria on achieving an effective and safe land transport system and replacing
the regional land transport strategy and the regional land transport programme with a
single regional land transport plan. It merges the national land transport strategy and the
Government policy statement on land transport funding into a single Government policy
statement on land transport. It also removes the obliga tion on regional transport
committees to include representatives of sector interests, instead leaving it to elected
representatives to decide whom they need to hear from.
The bill will also amend the Act’s f unding and planning provisions by enabling
future projects to be funded by borrowing, where there is a good case to do so and the
Minister of Transport a nd Minister of Finance agree. It is worth noting that in the last
year more than 5.5 million journeys have been taken on the Northern Gateway—a toll
road funded by debt through the previous Gove rnment. By repealing the regional fuel
tax provisions we acknowledge that this fo rm of taxation needs to  go, because its costs
would end up being spread across all regions.
The second significant area of change is the Act’s tolling provisions. The bill will
replace duplicative statutory te sts applying to the approval of  toll road schemes with a
single, high-level test requiring them to be efficient and effective. It will also rely on the
Privacy Act, rather than on an anonymous method of paymen t, to safeguard privacy. It
will reduce potential barriers to public-priva te partnerships in toll road building and
management by removing the requirement for special concession agreements. The final
change in this area is to enable the ex isting toll road in Tauranga—Route K—to be
brought under the toll road regime that applies to other toll roads in the country.
Finally, this bill establishes in legisla tion a new policy framework for planning and
contracting public transport,  known as the Public Transport Operating Model. This
follows a review of the Public Transpor t Management Act 2008 that found there was
little incentive for operators to invest in public transport services or for them to come up
with innovative ways for improving services . The legislation will require all public
transport services in a region to be segmen ted into units and provided under exclusive
contract to the regional council. Regional coun cils will be required to identify in their
regional public transport plans the units, th e policies on units, a nd the other public
transport services the region intends to financia lly assist. Services that are not part of a
region’s core public transport network will be exempt from operating under contract,
and will be identified on an exempt-services register held by the relevant regional
council.
This bill will repeal the Public Tran sport Management Act 2008 and carry over
relevant provisions into the Land Transport Management Act.
In closing, may I say that Parliament, in passing this bill, will ensure that New
Zealand has a durable piece of legislation that promotes an effective, efficient, and safe
land transport system. It also recognises th at New Zealanders want such a system.
Thank you. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: The Land Transport Management
Amendment Bill is a bad bill. National has corrupted the decision-making and resource-
allocation process for building new State highw ays. It is spending $1 billion a year on
seven hand-picked motorway projects. It ha s politicised the whole business of building
State highways in this country. Secondly, by pouring so much money into these white
elephant motorway projects it is locking th is country into a high- carbon, fossil-fuelled
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5103
dependent transport future. In the process it is neglecting public tr ansport, and it is
neglecting the maintenance of our State highw ays and our local roads. It is doing this
country a disservice. Those two qualities—the politicisat ion and corruption of our
decision making and resource allocation for bui lding State highways,  and its obsession
with roads at the expense of every other pa rt of our system—are the two qualities that
define this wasteful and mismanaged transport policy under this National Government.
This bill reflects that policy, and what it does is it sets in concrete the wasteful and
mismanaged approach that National has taken to transport. It se ts up a gerrymandered,
decision-making process for new transport proj ects. It puts into concrete its obsession
with roads at the expense of everything else , and it centralises more and more decision-
making power in Cabinet, away  from communities and away from the Public Service.
How does it do this? For a start, it gets rid of the existing purpose statement in the Land
Transport Management Act. Currently, the Land Transport Management Act’s purpose,
in section 3(1), is “to contribu te to the aim of achieving an  affordable, safe, responsive,
and sustainable land transport system.” Well, under this bill that is gone—it is gone. Let
us apply the “Holiday Highway” test to this  provision in this bi ll. Is the “Holiday
Highway” affordable—$1.7 billion for a duplicate route that, at  best, will slice 5 to 10
minutes off the journey between Auckland an d Wellsford? Is it safe? No, because a
$400 million job would actually fix the accident  black spots much more cheaply and
much faster. Is it responsive? No, it is not responsive to our country’s transport needs. Is
it a sustainable transport solution? No, it cer tainly is not. It is an overpriced, gold-
plated, duplicate motorway route.
OK, what else does it do? There are five tran sport objectives that also appear widely
in the Land Transport Management Act. Th ey are set out in section 14(a)(ii): “(A)
assisting economic development: (B) assis ting safety and personal security: (C)
improving access and mobility: (D) protecti ng and promoting public health: (E)
ensuring economic sustainability;”. They are five criteria that should be the guiding
principles of our transport system. Under this bill th ey are gone; they are gone by
lunchtime. Let us apply the “Holiday Hi ghway” test again. Does the “Holiday
Highway” assist economic development? The Minister of Transport likes to say that it is
going to solve all the economic problems of Northland. For $1.7 billion you could buy a
lot of high-quality economic development in Northland. Would the “Holiday Highway”
assist safety and personal security? No, we ha ve already talked about the fact that the
Operation Lifesaver alternative for $400 m illion would solve the safety problems on
that road. Does it protect and promote publ ic health? No. Is it a model of economic
sustainability? No, it is the opposite. If th e Act was used properl y, these principles,
these criteria would mean that projects that  meet those criteria would be prioritised. But
this Government’s approach is to make the land transpor t management legislation less
sustainable, less economically  viable, and less concerned wi th sustainability and with
public health.
The project level decision-making criteria unde r this bill—the criteria that we have
been discussing—are swept away, and they are replaced with three criteria that this
Government is using to drive its agenda of the roads of na tional significance. What are
those criteria? First, to give effect to th e Government policy statement—all right? So if

items.speaker: Gerry Brownlee says
items.text: “Yes, we’re going to build  the roads of national significance”, he
has a tick in the first box. Wh at is the second criterion? Eff ectiveness. Well, what is the
definition of effectiveness? It is whether it will deliver on the strategic fit. So the second
criterion is whether it will deliver what Gerry Brownlee wants! OK, two ticks in the
first two boxes. The third criterion is efficiency , or the benefit-cost ratio. That Minister
does not even believe in the benefit-cost ra tio, because the other day in this House he
gave an entire speech to the House saying: “Actually, don’t pay too much attention to
5104 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 11 Sep 2012
the benefit-cost ratio, because it is not very important.” So the three criteria are—first,
what is the Government’s policy statemen t? Let us build the roads of national
significance. What is the second criterion? How good the project is at delivering on the
Government’s policy. What is the third crite rion? The benefit-cost ratio. The Minister
does not even believ e in it. So the P ūhoi to Wellsford “Holiday Highway” rates on the
first two criteria very poorly, and on the thir d criterion it is not even very good either,
yet it can still be funded.
This is how Gerry Brownlee and Steven Joyce have totally gerrymandered the
decision-making process for how they spend $1 billion a year of our taxes on white
elephant motorway projects. That is what th is bill is about. It enshrines a circular and
self-serving politicised decision-making model for how we spend billions of dollars of
taxpayers’ money. Any pretence of rationality  in the decision-maki ng process has been
dispensed with. Any expectation that our transport system will be integrated and
multimodal has been done away with, because under this bill the references to rail and
coastal shipping are be ing deleted from the purpose statement of the Land Transport
Management Act.
We have two other big objections to this bi ll. One is that it takes power away from
local communities. Does that surprise anybody ? This is the Government that killed
democracy in Canterbury and it does not give a damn about the democratic rights of
communities. Look at the local government legi slation that is before the House at the
moment. It is all about taki ng power away from the elected  representatives and local
communities. So it should not surprise us that in this bill the Government abolished the
mechanism that would allow communities to use a regional fuel tax that was introduced
by the last Labour Government to ensure that  communities at least had the potential to
raise money in their own communities and to exercise some autonomy about their
transport priorities. Even t hough the current legislation keep s power in the hands of the
Minister, that is not enough for him. That Go vernment wants to abolish altogether the
right and the opportunity to institute a regi onal fuel tax. That provision is all about
giving the two-fingered salute to Auckland, be cause that Minister has not only already
said it cannot have a regional fuel tax to f und its transport agenda but also already ruled
out network charging—congestion charging. The Government does not want Auckland
or any other community to have any autonomy in their transport priorities.
The bill also reduces the obligation to consult communities on regional transport
plans, but that is academic because under this Government there is no money available
to fund local transport projects anyway, b ecause he has spent it all on the roads of
national significance.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: That’s utter rubbish.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: It is virtually impossible to f und a new State highway project in
this country because there is no money left in the kitty. The third objection that we have
to this bill is that it allows the New Zeal and Transport Agency not just to borrow for
cash-flow smoothing, as it can already do, but  to borrow to increase the size of the
transport budget. It makes toll roads easier to implement and it also makes it easier to

of those three mechanisms. But we are oppos ed to a transport pol icy that blows the
budget on gold-plated, low-value projects, and then comes back asking to use the credit
card. This is a bad bill. It is  entirely consistent with this Government’s wasteful and
mismanaged transport policy, and Labour will not be supporting it.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: First, before I talk too much
about the Land Transport Management Amendment Bill, I just want to  say that a lot of
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5105
the information that that last member, Phil Twyford, said was simply incorrect. There

I want to take just one example, and we can use this example to look at the

I want to see those Opposition parties come  to Hamilton and say what they say in

That road is crucial for the growth of our  city going forward. We will fight in this

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Nine—nine people went on it. Th at is the reality of public

But let us have a look at what Hamiltonian s actually want. They  want growth, they

The road to give them that. They are gett ing the link to Auckland, and they are getting

This is a good bill, and I implore anybody who has any problem with that to come to

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: This piece of
legislation, the Land Transport Management Amendment Bill, is typical of a
Government that is either ignorant of , or deliberately blind to, the long-term
consequences of the decisions it makes toda y. This piece of legisl ation does nothing to
support good-quality transport infrastructur e in New Zealand. Normally with the
National Party what we say is that it narrows its view simply to a thin economic
analysis of anything—anythi ng the National Party does. It overrides the social
implications. It overrides the environmental implications. But in this legislation it has
narrowed things so far that there is not even economic criteria any more in its decision
making around transport infrastructure. The only criterion is whether these projects fit
National Party policy. That is the only criterion that the New Zealand Transport Agency
will have to consider when it is deciding whether it should be building transport
infrastructure. But that is wrong, because not  only do we need economically sensible
and viable infrastructure but we need our infrastructure to be socially viable and
environmentally viable as well.
I want to go through the criter ia that are currently in th e Act and that this National
Government is going to get rid of, and cons ider what the impact will be on our nation.
The first criterion is to give effect to the G overnment policy statement. That one gets to
stay, and, as my colleague Phil Twyford pointed  out, the only thing that that means is
“Does it fit the Government’s policy?”. Wh ether the Government’s policy makes any
sense at all on economic, social, or environmen tal criteria, does it fit the Government’s
policy? Tick—that one fits. Is it affordable? That is a question the National Party should
always be asking. Is it afford able? Well, we have already s een what this Government’s
view is on transport infrastructure. It does not matter whether it is affordable. As long as
it is a road, then build it. Build the darn thing, whether we can afford it or not. Its view
is “Gold plate it, build it with eight lanes or 20 lanes, who care s! As long as it is a road,
we will build it if we are in the National Party.” Is it integrated? Well, it does not matter
any more whether the transport infrastructure is integrated, because there will be only
one form of transport infrastructure, and that is the roads.
Is it safe? We have already seen what this  National Party thinks of road safety and
transport safety. Mr Bridges should be interest ed in this. He is, of course, the Associate
Minister of Transport. I was in his electorate the other day, and I was talking to people
about transport infrastructure and transport funding. Do you know what the council told
me? It told me how its funding for road safety  promotion had been cut, as 75 percent of
its work had been funded by the New Zeal and Transport Agency and now barely 50
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5107
percent of the work is being funded by th e New Zealand Transport Agency. That has
resulted in a net cut in road transport safe ty promotion activities by the council in Mr
Bridges’ region. Those activities are not unde rtaken just for fun. They are undertaken
because there is an evidence base behind them that says that they improve road safety.
This Government has no interest in road sa fety. It is cutting the funding already, and it
is going to take the criterion that building transport infrastr ucture should be safe out of
the legislation. Is it sustainable? Well, we know that the Government is not interested in
sustainability. Does it assist economic de velopment? Well, as my colleague Phil
Twyford also pointed out, the Minister of  Transport does not even care about benefit-
cost ratios. He does not care about econo mic sustainability. He does not care about
affordability. He cares just about building roads.
Here is the one that I am really upset about.  It is the criterion that asks whether it
protects and promotes public health. This may sound like a bit of a tangent, but there are
four huge looming costs to our health syst em. They are confron ting us right now and
they are going to confront us even more in the future. One of them is cancer, the second
is cardiovascular disease, the third is diabetes, and the fourth is respiratory disease. I am
not sure whether there is much of a link be tween transport infrastructure and cancer,
although I would not be surprised if there is  one, but there certainly is a link between
transport infrastructure and our ability to tackle cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and
respiratory disease. We need more investme nt in active transport. Cycling and walking
as genuine transport options need to be invest ed in. If we want pe ople to change their
behaviour, if we want people to  move to rail or walking or  cycling, then we have to
build decent infrastructure that actuall y entices them and makes it useful and
worthwhile for them to undertake those forms of transport.
So, in the interests of public health, in th e interests of saving our health dollars and
making sure that our health resources are available to the people who need them, we
need to be building transport infrastruc ture that supports good health and supports
people so that we can reduce the incidence of  cardiovascular disease, and the same with
diabetes. Respiratory disease is  an issue that th is Government completely overlooks in
its health policy, but, again, the emissions fr om vehicles and the location of transport
infrastructure is an important factor in the incidence of respiratory disease. If we could
do more with that, again, we would be sa ving our nation a lot of money and we would
be doing a lot of good. We woul d have healthier, more pr oductive, better-off people in
our country. But these are things that this  Government is either ignorant of or
deliberately blind to.
Social responsibility—Mr Bennett talked about his pet transport project and his
hatred of a rail link between Hamilton and Au ckland. Well, my pet transport project at
the moment is the rail link between Palmer ston North and Wellingt on, which is very
similar to the proposed link between Hamilton and Auckland. Many people use that link
every day. For many people that is their sole way of getting to work and getting to the
job that happens to be in Wellington when  they live further up the line. For many of
those people, the loss of the train will mean th e loss of the ability to have that job. They
will either have to move from where they are at the moment into Wellington, or they
will have to give up that job and get a job somewhere else. Not everybody has a driver’s
licence. Some people—and this might come as  a bit of a shock to this Government—
have disabilities that prevent them from being able to drive a car; therefore, they need
alternatives, choices, options in transport infrastructure. But this bill is not about options
or choice in transport infrastructure. This is about the National Party’s narrow focus on
its roads of national significance.
Finally, there is environmental responsibil ity. Well, we know that public transport,
particularly rail, uses signifi cantly fewer resources than priv ate car-based transport. So
5108 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 11 Sep 2012
in the long-term environmental interests of th is country, we need to  be building better
public transport infrastructure. But this Gove rnment simply is not interested. It is a
conservative Government that is not interest ed in trying to lead  change. It is not
interested in trying to improve our nation. It is not interested in trying to improve our
economy. It is not interested in trying to improve the nation’s health. It is simply
interested in supporting the status quo and c ontinuing on with tired old ways of doing
things.
This is not a piece of legislation that will take New Zealand forward. It is a piece of
legislation that simply reinforces the Government’s desire to pursue a policy that makes
no economic sense, no social sense, and no environmental sense. We need better
thinking from our Government on transport in frastructure. We need a Government that
is thinking about the future and is interest ed in building an integrated and responsive
transport system, not one that is stuck in the old ways and the ideas of the past—the
think-big projects that the National Party is so well-renowned for. We do not support
this legislation.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: I rise on behalf of the Green Party to speak on
the Land Transport Management Amendment Bill. I do have quite a lot to say about this
bill. I will start by saying that it is really  a shame that the Government is missing this
incredible opportunity that we have in transport policy to achi eve the goal that it says it
wants to achieve, which is economic producti vity. We have the opportunity to build a
consensus, really, across Parliament to achie ve what all New Zealanders really want
from their transport system.
But, unfortunately, as was well articulated  by David Bennett, this Government is
stuck in the past. It is stuck in 30 years ago. He said that he was so happy that finally the
Waikato region was going to be getting the Waikato Expressway, a project that the
region has been advocating for for 30 year s—30. I think that speaks volumes about
where the Government is placed in terms of its transport thinking. It is stuck in the past.
The Green Party will not be supporting this bill—not because everything in the bill is
bad; some things are, arguably, quite good. Bu t when you take it in the context of the
current evidence-free transport policy and priorities, the changes that this bill makes
could allow some monumentally bad projects  to go ahead. That is, firstly, because the
bill allows for additional borrowing to pay for transport infrastructure. It allows for
borrowing over and above covering cash flow . At a time when the Government is
arguing that we need to sell strategic assets that are providing a h ealthy return, in order
to supposedly pay down debt, the same Govern ment is gearing up to borrow billions to
pay for uneconomic motorways. It is really tragically ironic that it is going to be
borrowing to pay for motorways that will not  even deliver the economic development
that it says it wants. The idea that the co st of infrastructure with long-lasting
intergenerational benefits could be spr ead over the years through borrowing is not a
terrible idea in and of itself. However, th is Government is prio ritising very bad State
highway projects that simply do not make economic sense. They certainly will not
substantially benefit future generations. So in this context, borrowing is extremely
dangerous. It is going to saddle future generatio ns with debt for projects that they will
not even benefit from.
The proposed legislation also opens the doors to public-private partnerships, and,
really, this is just a back-door way of borrowi ng. It is definitely still borrowing, but it is
keeping that debt off the Government books in the short term. I think that when we look
overseas at examples of public-private partners hips, particularly in respect of transport
infrastructure, what we find is that they are extremely damaging for the public sector
and they are extremely costly for the taxpa yer. We compiled rese arch on Australian
public-private partnership roading projects  that should be highly relevant to the
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5109
Government’s plan to use public-private part nerships to fund some of its roads of so-
called significance. Here is just one example: the CLEM7 Tunnel in Queensland. The
initial forecast cost was $1.2 billion. The actu al cost was $3 billion. The traffic forecast
at opening was 60,000 vehicles. The actual traffic during a lower toll period—this is the
peak—was 34,000 vehicles. That is about half  of what was forecast. The forecast for
2012—this year—was 100,000 vehicl es. And if you can believe it, the number of
vehicles using this project has fallen even further to 28,000. That is about a quarter of
what was forecast to use the project.
If you look at all of these Au stralian public-private partnership roading projects over
the last few years, you will see that they ar e all, basically, debacles. If you look at the
literature from Europe as well,  you see consistently that th ere is an ove r-prediction of
the benefits of roading proj ects through public-pri vate partnerships and toll roads, in
particular. The reason for this is actually really understandab le. It is that the entire
methodology that we have used in our transp ort planning for the past 50 years or more
is actually biased towards cars. It overesti mates the benefit of improvements that allow
more vehicles to flow through an area, and it underestimates the cost.
If we look at the actual evidence, then wh at we can understand, in a way that really
the National Party should be able to understa nd, is that there are a large number of
market distortions in our transport networ k. That has led to an extremely unbalanced
transport system, which, in the case of New Zealand, is very, very costly, and it is going
to become even more costly as we face rising fuel prices. We have the opportunity to do
things differently: to spend less money and to achieve the tr ansport outcomes we
want—the efficiency and the effectiven ess. We have the opportunity to reduce
congestion—spending less money and investing mo re in trains and buses. I am really
sorry that David Bennett is not here, because I think that if he actually looked—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Excuse me. Sorry, Mr Speaker. The previous speaker,
David Bennett, mentioned that the reality of  public transport was that people did not
take it and it required huge subsidies. But I think he has not actually looked at the
numbers, because in Auckland, for exampl e, public transport patronage has been
growing extremely fast, and patronage on the ra il network, in particular, is almost 30
percent higher than what was modelled by Auckland Transport’s model 2, which is the
public transport four-stage model’s demand for public transport and road projects.
At this point in time, when the Government is arguing that we need to reduce debt, at
the same time it is taking the exact opposite ap proach to transport infrastructure. There
could not be a more opportune time to actuall y reduce the amount of money that we are
spending on transport infrastructure and make it smarter, make it more effective, and
make it more targeted.
There were a few interesting observations in  the board paper that went to the New
Zealand Transport Agency about public-private partnerships, which are quite relevant to
this bill, as this bill is going to allow pub lic-private partnerships. Now we see that the
New Zealand Transport Agency is actually already preparing a business case for public-
private partnerships for certain roading proj ects. One of them was that Transmission
Gully obviously is not a good option for a publ ic-private partnership, even though the
Government has been talking about it being an option. The reason it is not a good option
for a public-private partners hip is that it does not ha ve a good business case. Every
Government analysis of that motorway proj ect has shown that there simply is not the
demand to justify the tolls that would be needed to pay for the project. So what does
that tell you? It tells you that, actually, the project is not economically viable. Going to
the private sector is not going to make viable  a project that is not  economically viable.
All it is going to do is take the risk and put  it on to the public. Actually, we have seen
5110 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 11 Sep 2012
that the model of public-private partners hips that the Government is actually
investigating does exactly that. It is called the availability payment model, which means
that tolls go to the Government, and the Government pays the private companies an
annual payment for building and maintaining th e road. This model puts all the risk of
low patronage on the Government and on the taxpayer, which we have seen in Australia
and in Europe, where, consistently, toll ro ads have less patronage and lower revenue
than what was forecast in the business model.
All the Green Party is asking for, really, is some economic rationality and evidence
to be applied to transport po licy, in a way that, really, the Government should be quite
open to. I would be quite happy to sit down wi th the Government and help it, because I
know that I have more expertise in this area  than it does. I am r eally interested in
working with the Government, because I ge nuinely believe that Government members
are going to live to see the day when ever yone in New Zealand realises that these
projects were a terrible waste of taxpaye rs’ money. They are goi ng to regret ever
supporting them. These roads will be like the motorways in Greece, which are
completely empty, cost billions of dollars, and did noth ing—nothing—to create
economic growth. That is very understandable, because once you have an existing road
network, the benefits of replacing or duplica ting a link diminish as time goes on. If you
were putting a brand new link in where there was no road before, maybe there would be
some economic benefits. But there are al ready roads between Auckland and Hamilton.
There are already roads between P ūhoi and Wellsford. The marginal cost of duplicating
that road is enormous, and the benefit is so tiny, because it is only a few minutes saved.
I would like to conclude by saying that the Green Party will not be supporting this
bill, until such time as the Government can  demonstrate that it is capable of an
economically rational transport policy. Thank you.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak on
this bill, the Land Transport Management Amen dment Bill. I think it is a bill that will
go down very well in this House once it ha s been through the fu ll select committee
process, once all parities have had an oppor tunity to fully cons ider the exceptional
benefits that can come from the bill, a nd once we have had an opportunity to go out
there and consult with the public on the benefits of the bill.
Approximately $3 billion annually from cen tral government is spent on transport,
and from local government approximately $1.5 bi llion. We need to ensure that we are
getting the best value for money with our trans port regime that is in place. We need to
also ensure that we lower the compliance co sts where we can, and this bill seeks to do
that.
I want to pick up on a few comments about the roads of nationa l significance, and
particularly on one I heard from Julie Anne  Genter just before. She was making some
comments about Greece and about how we may run into a situation where we end up
with motorways that are empty. I have to sa y that I realise she is  a little newer to
Auckland than I am, but I do not know any motorways in Auckland that are empty,
except in the dead of the night.
Aucklanders, in particular, along with  many, many New Zealanders around the
country, are crying out for even greater i nvestment in infrastructure—transport
infrastructure—around the count ry. They are crying out fo r greater investment in
roading infrastructure around this country. Ne w Zealanders have e ndorsed our plan for
the roads of national significance. They  have welcomed th e roads of national
significance policy.
As David Bennett has spoken about, people in parts of the country have been waiting
years for some of these projects to go ahea d. Let us remember that 92 percent of freight
in this country moves on roads. Let us re member that we want to build a stronger
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5111
economy in this country. Let us remember th e economic potential that these roads of
national significance will help to open up. Let us remember the New Zealanders who
rely on good quality infrastructure to operate their businesses, to get to work, and to get
their families to and from engagements ar ound their cities and around the country. New
Zealanders are welcoming this policy, and we are proud to stand behind it.
The great panacea, the grea t project that the Opposition and some people in
Auckland are proposing to solve all the transp ort problems in Auckland is the central
business district rail loop. Let us remember th at in 2041 the central bus iness district rail
loop will remove only 1,400 cars from the road out of 29,000 cars that will be travelling
on the road. Let us remember that their great hope for transport change in Auckland
would see transport benefits of only a bout $300 million to $400 million, based on an
approximately $3 billion project.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: What’s your alternative, Jami? What’s your alternative?

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: It is the projects that we are spending money on, Mr Twyford,
the projects that we are putting funding into. It is the $12 billion that this Government is
investing in roads of nationa l significance, the $3 billion that we spend on transport
every year—the $3 billion that is going into be tter quality infrastructure, something that
the Labour Government underfunded, underspent  on, and did not put a priority on,
which New Zealanders are crying out for and are looking to this Government to
continue. The roads of national significance policy is worthwhile continuing. It has been
endorsed by the voters at elec tion time, and they will be able to see it implemented
further through the passage of this bill.
There are other important provisions in this bill around changing the purpose, and
getting a more effective, efficient, and sa fe transport system. By  combining planning
documents, we will see more efficiency ga ined. By giving the New Zealand Transport
Agency the opportunity to borrow further if th e opportunity arises for future projects to
be looked at earlier than expected, and by simplifying the tolling process that
organisations have to go through if they wish to consider a tolling project, the bill will
enable more cost-effective tolling projects to be proceeded with.
This is a good bill. It deserves to be supported by Opposition members. If they do not
support it tonight, they should at least look at it properly through the select committee
process. If anyone will be ashamed at the end of this process, it will be those people if
they do not support a good piece of legislati on that allows greater investment in
important transport infrastructure around the country.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak on
the Land Transport Management Amendment Bill.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: That’s not this bill!

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I must say after listening to the honourable Mr David Bennett
speaking—do not worry, Mr Bridges, we w ill get to you. We will cross your bridge
when we come to it. I will say that after listening to the honourable David Bennett I am
sure that Vogel would be rolling in his grav e to see the chairman of the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee so blinkered, so blinded, so averse to common-sense
transport infrastructure such as rail. It is  very interesting, because the honourable David
Bennett has obviously been taki ng note of the Prime Minister, “Mr Spray and Walk
Away”. He has certainly given a big spray to those KiwiRail wo rkers who are losing
their jobs, and to those pe ople in Gisborne, the 10,800 peopl e who signed that petition
that the Transport and Industrial Relations  Committee decided to just ignore. His
comments really do cast serious doubts on the competency of the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee, and its ability  to be fair and true and to deliver
something other than party-based outcomes, because we all know that the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee is heavily weighted in the Government’s favour.
5112 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 11 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Oh well, that’s why there are rotten sleepers!

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: As I said, Mr Bridges, we will talk about rotting sleepers. I
will talk to you about them later.
But let us talk about tolling, because this bill is intended to facilitate and, in fact, ease
the facilitation of ro ad tolling. We in New Zealand Fi rst have real concerns about
expanding the role of toll roads. The notion of streamlining the process to introduce
more toll roads, we see as being against the wider public interest. Imposing tolls upon
key roads inhibits New Zealanders from tr avelling on them. We already know about all
the people who are living in poverty, although th at side of the House tends to turn a
blind eye to that. Similarly, the more to ll roads in New Zealand, the greater the
impact—and that is an adverse impact—on domestic and international tourism.
This Government needs to front up as to  why it is relaxing mechanisms surrounding
the introduction of toll roads. Could it possibly be for its Aussie mates in the Macquarie
Group? [Interruption] I notice in the bill—let us get around to Mr Simon Bridges. In the
bill, we see Route K there. I was hoping to see in this bill that the Government would be
taking over the debt from the Tauranga ra tepayers. There was its  opportunity to do
something for the people of Tauranga, but, no, it is not in there.
Let us talk about borrowing, because within  this bill is a fundamental change
allowing the New Zealand Transport Agency to  borrow to build roads. This is a very
significant change, and not one to be made li ghtly. What is missing is the justification
for this profound change. Where is the eviden ce that this is necessary? Where is the
cogent argument? Where is the compelling case for doing this? What is actually behind
the move? Earlier tonight, the members on that side of the House criticised this side of
the House for our attention to detail. We know that the devil is in the detail. Given the
state of the economy and our level of debt , giving the New Zealand Transport Agency
more borrowing powers needs to be fully explai ned and justified. It is quite simple. All
borrowing powers need to be carefully cons idered. The Government needs to be quite
clear. It needs to front up and tell us what is really going on.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Didn’t you listen to Gerry’s speech?

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: Well, I heard Gerry’s speec h, but I was wondering what
happened to the $12 billion set aside for the roads of national significance. What has
happened to the petrol taxes that we pay? Wh at has happened to the exorbitant prices
that New Zealanders are now forced to pay with road-user charges? What happened to
the jobs? Less debt, more jobs—was that not what the National Party campaigned on?
Now it is pushing forward with a bill that allows greater borrowing for the New Zealand
Transport Agency. So what are its priorities ? The bottom line is this: as it stands, New
Zealand First cannot rubber-stamp the Ne w Zealand Transpor t Agency having
additional borrowing powers without a full and proper explanation by this Government.
Let us go on to public-private partnerships. This bill will reduce potential barriers to
the use of public-private partnerships, and th e public should be very worried at this
development—very worried indeed. Private bus iness is there for a profit, and usually a
handsome profit. Much-touted public-private partnerships have been one of the great
ways, in fact, of hoodwinking the public. Th ey have often proved to be a bonanza for
private interests, but usually at the public expense.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: What a string of clichés.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: Well, what private business w ould want to get involved in a
public-private partnership if there were not a great profit in it for them? But when it all
goes bad, the taxpayer of New Zealand is left  footing the bill. When things go wrong it
is us, the taxpayers, who pay. We oppose the privatisation of Ne w Zealand’s roading
network by stealth. The last thing we need or want is for New Zealanders to be paying
some overseas corporation for the use of the roads here in our own country.
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5113
This bill does have a couple of merits , however. New Zealand First supports the
Government’s aim of reducing needless bur eaucracy, which often impedes large-scale
transport projects. However, New Zealand Fi rst cannot support this bill as it currently
stands. New Zealand First will not stand for relaxing regulations around road tolls, nor
will we idly stand by and allow this Govern ment to implement further public-private
partnerships at a greater cost to the taxpayer. Therefore, New Zealand First opposes this
bill.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: No, don’t sit down—there’s more. But wait, there’s more!

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: There is more coming, Mr Bridge s. You are going to have to
wait for that one, but it is very soon.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: What a pleasure it is on this occasion to follow
Brendan Horan. He has asked some questions . He nearly redeemed himself—nearly
redeemed himself—by saying that there were  two points that New Zealand First would
support in the Land Transport Management Am endment Bill. He got one out, but could
not bring himself to say the other. He could not bring himself to say the other, so I will
have to canvass a few, just to see whether these are what he w ould have supported. We
are not doing just roads; we have i nvested $4.6 billion in a 10-year KiwiRail
Turnaround Plan—
Simon O’Connor: How much?

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: —including $250 million—$4.6 billion, billion with a
“b”—over 2012-13. We have committed $1.6 billion to improve and electrify
Auckland’s rail system, and invest ed—wait for it—$500 million to upgrade
Wellington’s rail. We are already working well.
Why, we are asked by Mr Horan, is Nationa l doing this? It is because National is
committed to building a more competitive and productive economy, and we must get
the infrastructure right. We are building a better transport system, which is vital in order
to transform New Zealand’s future and to create more jobs with higher incomes. We are
committed to simplifying and to modernising New Zealand’s transport system so that it
is efficient, cost-effective, a nd fair for all users. I ask you, if this were an election year,
would these be things that New Zealand Firs t said it would espouse? Yes. Yes, they are
in keeping with its policy. I cannot see wh ere Mr Horan’s objections are coming from.
And the suggestion that somewhere behind it all there is a conspi racy does not quite
ring true. It does not quite ring true.
Let us just reflect on how we ll we have done with our infr astructure. I think back to
our forebears, our predecessors. I remember  Mr Holyoake saying—I am sure it shows
what age I am, I suppose—that we would ha ve a road to within  5 miles of every
primary producer. I used to go for a haircut 30 miles into Hokianga, on a metal road—
not much fun. We should enjoy what we have got in terms of good roading. New
Zealand has done remarkably well. I believe, and I stand to be corrected, that in terms of
mileage we have more sealed roads than Japan—certainly more per head of population.
New Zealand has done very, very well with it s infrastructure. This bill will improve
things even further. It seeks to deal with what is an important issue for all communities,
ensuring that our transport system is efficien t, cost-effective, and fair for all users. I
remember Mr Anderton finding, to his horror,  that there were insufficient roads in
Gisborne to get the timber to the mill. We need—

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: There’s insufficient rail in Gisborne, thanks to the National
Government.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, we have heard about rail. We heard a very, very
lucid piece from the chairman of the Tran sport and Industrial Re lations Committee, Mr
David Bennett, who spoke—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I wouldn’t call that lucid.
5114 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 11 Sep 2012

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, it was lucid, actually.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I think you mean loose.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: No, no, no, it was lucid. He rea lly got it together, and he
gave us the figures. He told us what wa s happening. Rail has a way to go. Well, I
believe in rail. The West Coast needs rail ve ry much indeed, such as the Midland Line
for taking the coal out. But it is a bit disturbing to find that it does not actually make
much money on the job.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Talk about the bill, Chris.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, we will talk about the bill, and I am glad—I am
glad—that there is such a demand to hear about it. The bill will require improvements to
central government’s planning and funding fr amework for land transport activity, as
well as changes to streamline the assessment of  toll road schemes and the creation of a
new policy framework for building long-term partnerships between  regional councils
and public transport operators and the public -private partnership system, which the
previous speaker had such a fear of. This bill handily covers those particular things.
The bill shows this Government’s commitment to getting the best value for dollar
and to removing ridiculous duplication, which ha s been allowed to clog the arteries of
public transport. I support this bill, and I want to leave room for other National speakers
to be able to speak about it. So I will cl ose by saying that I am supporting the bill
because I believe it to be noble of intent, fo rward of thinking, and realistic in its goal
seeking. Its goal is to ensure that the people of this nation get the best services. Thank
you.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I am pleased to take a call on the Land Transport
Management Amendment Bill. It is not the first one I have taken a call on in my time in
Parliament. I think this is No. 2. There was the Public Tr ansport Management Act as
well, which the Labour Government implemente d and which this bill actually repeals,
as I understand it.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I think this is the worst one.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Well, I am sure it is the worst one. I am going to talk about
how good the other ones are.
As always, we had a fantastic speech from David Bennett. One of the things I really
like about David Bennett—you know, he has got a lot of flaws, but on e of the things I
do like about him is he does tr y to promote his own area. He  does like to talk about the
Hamilton expressway an awful lot—an awful lot—but I was really interested, because
what he does not talk about is the problems with public transport in his own city. I was
really interested to see a press release fr om the Waikato Regional Council today saying
that passenger transport bus fares are going to  rise by 5 percent for children and adults
on the council’s rural services, which include Te Awamutu, Cambridge, Huntly,
Raglan, Paeroa, Morrinsville, and Taup ō. I know this goes into the areas of some other
members. There are other National MPs who are electorate members—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What does the member for Taupō think of that?

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Yes, well, the member for Taup ō is involved in that. But,
anyway, the reason I was saying this is that throughout New Zealand, public transport is
operating in an extremely c onstrained funding environment,  and as a region we are
being asked to do more with less, because  the Government has capped funding for the
next 3 years and has told th e council that it expects the amount of  money recovered
from fares to increase to 40 percent by 2017. So, you know, I would really like to hear
from the National members, the electorate MPs for those areas. They should stand up
and justify this bill on the basis that in their areas poor pe ople who live in rural
communities—the rural communities that th ey say they represent—are going to be
having to pay more for public transport.
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5115
What this bill does, of course, is repeal the Public Transport Management Act, which
had a lot to do with public tran sport and a lot to do with maki ng sure that we had better
public transport through councils. As I said, I would like to rehearse the history of the
Labour Government, because we had the fi rst Land Transport Management Act, in
2003. That was the biggest change in land tr ansport funding and management since the
1980s. Prior to that, the framework of la nd transport management and funding was
incredibly flawed. There was no strategic di rection. It did not al low an integrated
approach to be taken to land transport b ecause it focused on roading, and—hello—here
we are back at the beginning again. What was happening before that Act was we had no
long-term planning and the rules regardi ng the funding of public transport were
constraining and inflexible. So  that Act, along with the Public Transport Management
Act and also an amendment to the Land Transport Management Act in 2008, made
significant strides in our land transport systems, including public transport.
One of the significant things about th e Land Transport Management Act was
hypothecation.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Hypothecation?

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Hypothecation—that is right. That  changed the way that fuel
excise is used to provide more certainty  for future investment. It was a Labour
Government that brought about hypotheca tion. It augmented central government
transport funding through regional fuel taxe s, which allowed regions to fund more
projects, which of course this bill does away with. We increased investment in public
transport tenfold and funding for passenger transport services.
In case anyone forgets, it was Labour th at initiated double tr acking in Auckland,
electrification, the extension of passenger transport to other parts of Auckland, the
reopening of railway links, and the North Shore busway, which has been such a success.
I know my colleague Phil Twyford is keen to see that success replicated in his electorate
of Te Atat ū. Going down the western motorway it would be a wonderful thing, but I
fear we may have to wait for a Labour Government for that to happen. But he will
campaign. He will have—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Long time away, then.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Well, that is very nice of Maggie Barry, given that her—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Maggie, you got one; we want one too.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: That is right. That member’s electorate has one, so why can
west Auckland not have one? If this was not  such an ungenerous Government, it would
consider that.
So this bill undoes much of that really good work that was done over several years
under a Labour Government, under some fantas tic transport Minist ers, including the
Hon Annette King and others. In stead, it is being framed as being about streamlining
and increasing value for money, but all it doe s is open the door for borrowing for more
State highways, tolling, and public-private partnerships. It  is also about increasing
central government control over the transport system and making sure that local people
have almost no say. It is also about shar pening the focus on economic efficiency by
removing social and environmental criteria.
All you have to do is have a look at the difference in the purpose statement in this
proposed bill. Under the previous bill, there were a number of things, and my colleagues
have gone through them. Under the previous purpose statement the legislation had to
give effect to the Government policy statemen t; it had to be affordable, integrated, safe,
responsive, and sustainable; it  had to assist economic development, safety and personal
security, access, and mobility—I have not heard the words “mobility” and “access”
mentioned at all tonight; it does not matter,  does it—it had to protect and promote
public health, ensure economic sustainability, and it talked about social responsibility.
5116 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 11 Sep 2012
Public transport is a public good, and transport and access to transport is also a public
good.
In respect of environmental responsibility, I would have thought that in this time of
2012, even a National Government could brin g itself to say the words “environmental
responsibility”. Instead, what we have is a purpose statement that is reduced to so-called
streamlined project level decision-making criteria. Three things: give effect to the
Government policy statement, be effective, and be efficient. What a disgrace!

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: That just means: “Does Gerry want it?”.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: What?

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: It just means: does Gerry want it?

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Oh, does Gerry want it? Well, that seems to be the only
criterion that we have had for all of the roads of national signifi cance. Of course, the
Government has realised that those roads are far too expensive and it is going to have to
borrow to pay for them. It just will not accep t that some of the decisions it has made
around those are just ridiculous.
I suppose you could almost call this bill  the “Gerry Brownlee - Steven Joyce
Justification for Roads of National Significance—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: “Gerry-mandering”.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: A “Gerry-mandering Bill”. It is a “Gerry-mandering Bill” that
is all about sort of post—what is it? Post facto—post—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Ex post facto.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: That is the one. It is a justif ication for a real disaster of a
policy—a disaster of a policy—w hich is seeing gold-plated  roads being built up and
down the country. There is that smell of bitumen in the Minister’s nostrils.
What this bill is about doing is justifying the policy of roads of national significance,
doing away with the very balanced approach that we had under the previous Land
Transport Management Act and the Public  Transport Management Act, doing away
with a balanced approach to transport, and doing away with important things like
reference to integrated transport, coastal shipping, and rail. The only thing that seems to
matter to this Government is that everything has to go by road. It is so short-sighted—

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: So 1950s, that is right. It is so la st century. It is so last century,
as one of the Ministers said once, and I think that is a disgrace.
I am part of the Transport and Industria l Relations Committee. I am looking forward
to having a debate with David Bennett about why the people in his electorate are having
to pay more for their buses and why he keeps justifying the roads of national
significance, when the poor people in his area,  the people in rural areas whom he says
he represents, will not be able to afford to go on buses and will not be able to afford
public transport.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: In electorates like mine in the
Coromandel we like roads. Unlike the Greens,  we like roads because we need roads.
Roads are what provide us with  the wealth and the productivity  efficiency that we need
in our provincial and rural electorates around the countryside. The National Government
is committed to making a brighter future for all New Zealanders and we do that partly
by building a strong, bold, big, bright infras tructural network ar ound the country that
involves roads.
I want to commend my colleague David Benne tt, who happens to be chairman of the
Transport and Industrial Relations Committee, which will shortly consider this very
good bill, the Land Transport Management  Amendment Bill, for his passionate
advocacy on behalf of the Waikato Expre ssway. What a good local MP he is. What a
good local MP he is, that David Bennett. He spoke so vigorously, so passionately, about
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5117
the benefits that the Waikato Expressway will bring, unlike the Green member Julie
Anne Genter, who seemed to want to create for us a nirvana of a Green-inspired vision
of the world that sounded to me something akin  to the Amish state of  the South Seas. It
was going to be an Amish society without th e Bibles, however, but one where we were
on horses and carts, with those red safety triangles on the back of the little buggies. That
is what we would be driving around on, on our unsealed pathways around New Zealand,
if Julie Anne Genter and the Greens have their way.
So this is a wonderful piece of legislat ion, and the second good piece of legislation
that has been introduced tonight under the na me of Gerry Brownlee. It is about growing
a better future, a better infrastructure, for New Zealand. I rise to support the bill. I
commend this bill to the House, and I am looki ng forward to participating in the debate
at the select committee.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak on the Land
Transport Management Amendment Bill, and to reiterate Labour’s opposition to this
piece of legislation, which will only ever take us backwards. If ever there was a concern
about why the New Zealand Transport Agency should be given extra borrowing powers,
one does not have to look too far back in history to understand why, because this was
the Government agency that made a financial error in the last financial year of—wait for
it—$182 million. It miscalculated $182 million and had to get additional Crown
financing to cover that gap. That is the level of mistak e the agency made, and this
Government now wants to give it greater powers to borrow to cover its mistakes.
The principal question for me, in this legi slation, is how will this bill help the
regions? How will this bill help the regions? Coming from working actively in a
regional area, the region of Taranaki, home of the Ranfurly Shield and home of the
brave, I can say that it is a region that has suffered hugely from this Government’s
transport policies, or lack of priorities in roading and in transpor t. It has had little
support. There has been little support from this Governme nt for regional roading. This
bill represents a greater concentration of power, when the issue for regions at the
moment is just how much input and how much power lo cal authorities and their
transport committees can actually have. This bill represents a greater concentration of
power in the centre and in the roading agency, and that will not help a bit.
Let me talk about a couple of examples in Taranaki, which are issues that have been
longstanding, and where the local committ ee and the local community have long
expressed a need for priority and a need for funding. They are safety issues. One is the
Normanby Overbridge in South Taranaki. They  put up their submission to get it on the
plan this year and it was knocked back. This is  a bridge that is a d eath trap. It has killed
a couple of young chaps already—in fact, just recently. This is a community that is
hanging out for roading improvements. It will no t be that expensive. They have already
attempted to divert local money into what is a State highway to fix the problem, but
they cannot get it fixed and they cannot get the New Zealand Transport Agency on
board to fix it. The most rece nt long-term plan that the New Zealand Transport Agency
produced has not fixed the problem at all.  Then there is the road north of New
Plymouth, State Highway 3, which goes for about 100 kilometres. It has major
problems with paving, there is  no shoulder, there are issues  about the bridge abutments
and the uneven surface, and there has been no money at the centre for it. The region has
tried to use regional funding to fix up bits of that road, but it simply is not enough. What
will happen now, if this bill goes through as it is, is that we will just see an even greater
concentration of power in the centre and less voice for the local community.
5118 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 11 Sep 2012
Let us have a look at one aspect of this  bill: clause 61, which amends section 96.
Under section 96 at the moment there is a qu ite explicit and clearly set out approach to
be taken when the agency is considering the funding of ro ading. It requires the agency,
in terms of its operating pr inciples, to “exhibit a sense of social and environmental
responsibility”. That includes a host of things : that it avoids, to the extent reasonable,
adverse effects on the environment; that it ensure s, in relation to its functions and to the
extent practicable, it consults with persons a nd organisations in the region; that it takes
into account the views of the local commun ity; and that it meets the requirements of
consulting with local M āori. All of that goes in this bill—all of that goes in this bill. If
this bill does one thing th at is bad, amongst everything el se, it is that it guts the
opportunity for local communities to have a say and an input into the priorities for their
transport needs, and that is wrong.
It is characteristic of this Government in so many respects. It is not just in
Canterbury; not just in the Canterbury Regional Council. No w we are seeing it in this
legislation too—taking away the local voice, and taking away the voice of the people. It
has happened so commonly with this Gove rnment, in the way it operates and the
legislation that it is passing, and we are seeing it here now too. It is unnecessary and it is
bad. It is one reason why the Labour Party will be opposing this legislation.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia
ora. I rise to take a call on the Land Transport Management Amendment Bill or, as it
more accurately should be called, the “Land Transport (Put it on the Credit Card and
Pray for a Brighter Future) Bill”. This b ill—this bad bill—simply does a few bad things
for New Zealand. It does not go about transport the key way, which is that we should be
discussing how to get around. Let us not make  up stuff and exaggerate, as we heard
from the National backbench, about horse and carts. Let us have a discussion around
how we design our transport systems that work for us in 2012. How do we design a
transport system that is going to work for the future? How can we have a multimodal
system, where we have a role for road sa fety improvements, ra il, coastal shipping,
walking, and cycling to boost our economy and to get us around our cities cheaper and
faster, and how can we provide it?
The Government has not gone from that approach. It has gone from the Steven
Joyce, “Colossus of Roads”, transport approach, which is to put it on the credit card. He
has gone around the country spending $14 bi llion on just seven new, uneconomic
motorways, and now he has found that he has dug himself a fiscal hole. He has left the
mess for Gerry Brownlee, the current Minister  of Transport, and now the Government
has to put it on the credit card. The bill also streamlines toll roads in New Zealand—and
I want to quickly touch on the privacy impli cations there—and then reduces local input
in decision making, when it co mes to it. It is simply incr edible that in a time of
austerity, when we are facing nearly $70 billion in gross national debt, and when we are
seeing the Government cut various Budget lines , this Government is quite prepared to
put more uneconomic motorways on the credit card. It is simply mad, when we know
that some of them have negative benefit-cost ratios.
Take P ūhoi to Wellsford. Independent consulta nts found that it ha d a benefit-cost
ratio of 70c. This means that any member of the Government would get laughed out of a
board meeting if they were going to bo rrow a dollar and get only 70c in economic
return. It does not make sense. What we ar e seeing is a time of record high oil prices,
declining road traffic, and public transp ort patronage breaking  records and going
through the roof. This Government is looking towards the 1950s to borrow more for
motorways. It is like Julius Vogel in the 1870s borrowing billions to build bullock
tracks, not the high technology of the time. It does not make sense.
But what this bill also does is reduce the privacy of New Zealanders. This bill, quite
deliberately, in its streamlining of toll road s removes previous legislative requirements
11 Sep 2012 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 5119
for personal information to not be collecte d. It has raised the Privacy Commissioner’s
red flag. She is concerned, and we look forward to her submission to the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee. The question is why the Government is doing this. I
have not heard a single member on that side of  the House talk about this issue. It is
likewise with the Public Tran sport Operating Model change s. I have not heard anyone
on the Government side say why they are doing  it, because the truth is that they want
their mates—their mates who donate to them—t o cherry-pick the most profitable routes
and leave the least profitable routes up to the councils.
At the same time, this Government wa nts to take away the local community
representation—the non-voting members on re gional transport committees. It wants
Steven Joyce and Gerry Brownlee to tell all of our cities, including Coromandel, which
has had its local road budget slashed to pay for Auckland, to  pay for Wellington, and to
pay for Waikato, that there is no money for Coromandel. This is what we are seeing
going forward with road safety.
We could be spending that money on ro ad safety improvements. We could be
spending that money saving the Gisborne ra il line. We could be saving that money
getting a rail link between our  first-biggest and third-biggest cit y, but we cannot,
because Gerry Brownlee and Steven Joyce ha ve raided transport money and raided the
transport pantry. They have run out of mone y and now they have to put it on the credit
card. Now they are saying that your privacy  will not be respected, and your local
decisions will not be respected—in fact, th ey are going to take those people off the
regional transport committees.
At the same time, they are also saying to Auckland: “We are not going to let you
decide what you do with your transport money.”  They are explicitly stating in this
legislation that we cannot have regional fuel levies. If  Auckland wants to do it, if
Auckland wants to go forward, it should be ab le to do it. This Government is the block
to Auckland going forward, and it is going to get punished down the line.
At the last election the Green Party went  to the New Zealand electorate with a
modern plan for smart trans port that would have saved th e taxpayer money, that would
have paid down debt, and that would have i nvested a considerable share in the central
business district rail link, in light rail fo r Auckland, in rail, and in coastal shipping.
What we lack from this Government ar e road safety improvements, which would
actually save Kiwi lives now. There is a be tter way of doing it, and this bill is the
absolute worst way you would go about it. Kia ora, Mr Speaker.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): Look, the heart of this Land Transport
Management Amendment Bill is about efficien cy in transport, and I can think of no
better way to honour that than by supporting the bill and asking that it go to a vote.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Land Transport Management
Amendment Bill be now read a first time.
Ayes 61
New Zealand National 59; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 60
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Part y 14; New Zealand First 8; M āori Party 3;
Mana 1.
Bill read a first time.
Bill referred to the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

MOTIONS 
2012 Paralympic Games—Success of New Zealand Team 
Hon MURRAY McCULLY (Minister for Sport and Recreation) : I seek leave to 
move a motion without notice congratulating the Paralympic team on its performance at 
the recent Paralympic Games. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none. 
Hon MURRAY McCULLY: I move, That this House congrat ulate the members of 
the 2012 New Zealand Paralympic team on th eir outstanding performance, achieving 
six gold, seven silver, and four bronze medals and finishing ranked 21 st in the world.  
The 2012 New Zealand Paralympic campaign can be judged a real success, and on 
behalf of the Government I want to acknowledge all of the athletes who were members 
of the team and congratulate them collectively on their achievement.  
I want to mention in particular Sophie Pascoe, who added significantly to her 
previous successes on the international stag e, collecting three gold and three silver 
medals, and setting two new world records and one new Paralympic record. We saw 
outstanding performances from a number of ot her athletes who were  part of the New 
Zealand team. The achievement of 17 medals is all the more admirable when you note 
that there were only 24 in the team. On t op of that, New Zealand has come out as the 
leading nation per capita, up on third at the Beijing Paralympics.  
The 2012 Paralympics broke a number of reco rds, with 2.7 million spectators filling 
the various venues and more than $70 million ra ised in ticket sales. Both of these are 
unprecedented figures. Two hundred and fifty- one world records were broken over 11 
days. For our people to have succeeded in an environment this challenging is a very 
significant achievement indeed. I am theref ore pleased to offer on behalf of the 
Government our congratulations to all of the members of the 2012 Paralympic team as 
well as their coaches, support staff, and families, who played such an important part in 
their performance. 
DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) : I also would like to join in 
congratulating our Paralympic team. It was a great moment to able to stand here and say 
that today New Zealand is on top of the worl d, and that means that our medal total per 
capita was actually the best in the world, which is a remarkable achievement.  
The incredible performance of our paralympians in London has been something that 
has made us very, very proud. When our t eam comes home tomorrow it will bring with 
it 17 medals: six gold, seven silv er, and four bronze. That is  an absolute triumph, and it 
is a significant improvement on the Beiji ng Paralympics, when New Zealand was 
ranked third for medals per capita. This achievement reflects the hard work, the 
dedication, and the commitment of the Kiwi contingent.  
I would like to pay tribute to the efforts of  the entire team of  24 athletes, from 13-
year-old Nikita Howarth, who made her de but in swimming, to Jan Apel, who also 
made her Paralympics debut, in sailing at the age of 61, which is an enormous 
inspiration to us all. Our athletes perf ormed brilliantly across all of the events—
swimming, cycling, rowing, athletics, eque strian, sailing, and shooting—and I would 
particularly like to mention the achievem ents of Christchurch swimming sensation 
Sophie Pascoe, who won a medal in every event that she ente red. It was a proud 
5032 Motions 11 Sep 2012 
moment to see Sophie carry the flag into  the stadium for the closing ceremony. She 
absolutely deserved the honour. Our team ove rall did us proud. I was lucky enough to 
meet swimmer Mary Fisher at the Upper Hutt “cossie club” just before she left for the 
games, and I was struck by her commitment and the amount of hard work that she had 
put in to get where she was. She went on to win four medals, including a gold.  
One disappointment for me, however, and, I am sure, for many other New 
Zealanders, was that we were not able to  see many of these ach ievements of all our 
team live on television, as people did in other countries. We had to rely on delayed 
coverage or an international feed that did not focus on our Kiwi team. That is a shame, 
and I hope it is different for the next Paraly mpics. To be able to see our athletes 
triumphing over personal adversity to excel at their chosen sport is an inspiration to us 
all.  
So I would like to thank our athletes and pay special tri bute to all the unsung heroes 
around them: the coaches, the physios, the volunteers—all those people who put in 
enormous amounts of time so they could succeed. Thank you and congratulations on 
your success. 
KEVIN HAGUE (Green) : I wish to add the Green Party’s congratulations to our 
Paralympic team. To compete at the elite level in any sport requires determination, 
commitment, and sacrifice. Our Paralympic team had those attributes in spades. These 
Paralympics perhaps mark the point not only  in this country but  in others around the 
world where Paralympic sport is seen as el ite sport in its own right. That is a great 
milestone to have reached. I share the concer ns that David Shearer has just expressed 
about the decisions made by th e sports editors of our medi a. I cite Richard Boock’s 
column in the Sunday Star-Times  where he noted that th e media had misjudged the 
public mood, our desire to actually see our paralympian team competing on the world 
stage. Our team has been an inspiration to people living with disabilities. They have 
been an inspiration to thos e of us who look out the window  and decide we do not want 
to go to training, because it is too hilly, or it  is raining, or we just cannot be bothered. 
They have also unlocked a gateway for the New Zealand public in that we may finally 
now honour the rights of people with disabilities to be full members of our own society. 
Thank you. 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First) : The London Paralympics were 
a great success and particularly so for our New Zealand team. New Zealand First stands 
with all parties here today in congratulati ng our paralympians on their efforts and great 
achievements. 
Hon TARIANA TURIA (Co-Leader—M āori Party): I am really delighted to be 
able to share with every party in the House today the pride and excitement that we have 
experienced over these last 2 weeks with the amazing succes s of the New Zealand team 
at the London 2012 Paralympics. Yesterday as I landed at Whakat āne Airport I arrived 
at the same time as a reception was being extended to welcome home Ngāti Awa and Te 
Arawa mountain bike superstar, Karen Hanl en. In reflecting on her meteoric climb to 
the London Paralympics, she said her appro ach was built upon the philosophy that pain 
is temporary and pride is for ever. It is a philosophy that every single one of the 24 New 
Zealand athletes who competed at the Paralympics has demonstrated in abundance. 
These stars of many sports, including cy cling, shooting, swimming, and shot-put, 
have shown the world that even when others have said they could not, the determination
